old_title: South Africa v Australia: wet outfield causing delays in second men's cricket Test, day two - live
new_title: South Africa close on 97-5 against Australia on day two of second men's cricket Test after rain delays - as it happened
old_text:
More good news from Gqeberha! The players have arrived at the ground having been at the hotel all day. Buckle up folks, we could well have some Test cricket to watch in the not too distant.
I tell you what though, there are promising signs at the ground, the stumps are being readied and pitch lines painted! Hopefully we will see some action in a little over half an hour, wouldn't that be something!?
There will be another inspection at 3pm local time - about 35 minutes from now. The perils of trying to play Test cricket in South Africa in October eh. It is sunny at the ground now but the damage may already have been done depending on how good the drainage is. Well, we keep our extremities crossed.
Elsewhere in the Cricverse - Harry Brook has been speaking ahead of England's white ball tri tournament in Pakistan:
The good news is that the umpires are out in the middle doing an inspection. The bad news is that you can clearly see water squelching out from underneath their shoes as they walk on the outfield. That's not a good sign.
Thanks Geoff and hello all. We watch and we wait, will the big mop up job of Gqeberha 2026 result in some play on day two? We watch and we wait... there's an inspection due in 15 minutes so fingers crossed we are getting closer to some actual Test cricket action.
Any thoughts, theories and general patter please do send my way. Let's keep this OBO afloat.
I have probably said all that I can say about rain today, and the only thing undampened is our enthusiasm for Test cricket. So I will hand you over to James Wallace, who is an entertaining type, so please do send him some emails so that he has something to talk about. Today, the whole arena is yours. Cheerio.
So where does that leave us? Inspection at 14:15 local means the earliest play could start would be 15:00, and that's only if the ground has dried enough. So we're going to start at least five hours late, which means losing at least three hours of match time. They might get two to three hours of play if the light stays good tonight.
A day and a half taken out of the Test match then. That does leave time for a result if the match moves quickly, but there might be more rain later in the week.
"I wouldn't be astonished if Lyon retires from Test cricket a little sooner than people might be expecting," emails Paul. "For athletes who've performed at a very high level for a long time, one of the hardest things to accept seems to be when they're no longer an automatic selection, and while in Lyon's case that's been for reasons beyond his influence, he doesn't strike me as someone who'll be content with a here-and-there role."
I've wondered that too, and also whether this chop-change thing is making him less effective. There are mutterings that he's contributing in the margins, and his last bag of wickets was over two years ago in Wellington. But by leaving him out this many times recently, is Australia hurting themselves by having a less confident, less settled bowler in their line-up when they do need him?
In Jamaica or in Brisbane, did the fourth seamer win them the Test? No. Would they have won with Lyon in the team? Probably. So is there actually a benefit to the configuration without him? Debatable, but there is an observable negative if you're unsettling a vital player in the medium term.
"In the old days, the general rule was three seamers and two spinners, which could still be managed if at least two of the bowlers were proper batters, but even more so if the wicketkeeper was batting in the top five," writes John Starbuck. "Now, the ball can vary so much more from the faster bowlers - swing, reverse swing, knuckle and so on - that the mystery element of spin and flight aren't needed. Or so the selectors seem to think. Personally, I want to see at least one specialist spinner in every side, just to change the nature of the game."
Yes, so often the key is the ability to change the type of bowling that a set batter is facing.
I'm told that they did have an inspection. The umpires wandered about and talked to the ground staff. Often after prolonged rain like this, the covered square is ok but the outfield beyond the covers is a problem. Still nobody has adopted the Sri Lanka method of having 300 blokes covering the entire field.
Luca Human writes in. I've met a few South Africans with the surname Human recently, having never seen it before the last year or so, which I'll admit does make me suspicious that they're aliens trying to blend in, who didn't quite understand the context when choosing a last name that they thought would be innocuous. Anyway. I won't take you to our leaders, because they're largely absolutely awful.
"South African living here in France who overslept because a) school holidays and b) no cricket. I wanted to know regarding the 2027 CWC, if you think crowds in SA will be respectable? What of Zim and Namibia?"
Well, in the frame of my post about CSA earlier, the ICC does have a marketing budget. A titanic one. And the ICC is essentially an events company. So they will leave no doubt that there is a World Cup on. Ticket registration is already open, the schedule is already done, and apparently numbers have been good already on people making requests.
Not every game will be full, of course, with India games the most popular and so on. But I think that a South African World Cup is a very appealing tourist trip for a lot of Brits and Aussies and New Zealanders. There are also big expat communities of those people in the UK and Europe, who might fly down. Then there are the large communities of South Africans who have Indian or Pakistani backgrounds, so they'll also be interested.
I have faith the crowds will be good in South Africa, and I hope that for the handful of games in Namibia, novelty value will get people along, and for Zimbabwe, they play all their games at home, so that will be a draw.
Plus, can't tell you what a difference it makes to tourists to have a year to plan the trip, with confidence that the schedule won't change, as opposed to all the recent World Cups in India where we get the schedule six weeks out, and inevitably change a few games even after that point. They are truly disastrous hosts from the perspective of people wanting to attend games, so overseas tourists just don't bother.
"Shout out to Disney," writes John Stewart. Unlikely to be that one, no. John Oliver might be watching the cricket with Zaltzman, but he'd be the only late night host.
"They bought the NZ broadcast rights for the SA test series; they mucked up the calendar, and had the test match scheduled to start today rather than yesterday. So they didn't actually broadcast day 1.
"After about 40 minutes on the blower last night, I convinced the customer support person that cricket goes for five days, so it's not five different games, and that it wasn't a time-zone muck up on my part; Joshy was already throwing down his third. Eventually after getting me to turn it off and on a couple of times, she was just like 'Oh well, you should be able to watch it tomorrow I guess'.
"Imagine having so much money you buy the broadcast rights to a test series, then don't even notice you're not broadcasting it. That's what you and Adam should have done in Pakistan that time. Ultimate flex."
That is pretty impressive. I can assure you that we did notice we were broadcasting, it was among the most stressful experiences of my admittedly quite pleasant life.
That story is here, if you want something to fill half an hour of your rain delay time. Mike Williams is a brilliant audio doco maker.
Ground staff are repainting the pitch lines, which is great news. There's an inspection due in about 45 minutes, given how wet the ground got. With any luck, that would then mean action in one hour and 45, with the lunch break considered to have been taken, and we could get straight into a 2.5 hour session. We'll see.
"Fast bowlers don't eat as many pies or neck as many beers as they used to back in the day, so the role of the spinner to hold up an end is diminished these days," suggests David Blackah. "Also drop in pitches don't take turn until days 4 & 5 and it's often all over by then."
There is something to that last bit. Also the fact that teams now bowl about 70 overs a day even when it's clear and sunny.
Still, I don't buy the argument that because a game may be shorter, you don't need a spinner. If it ended in three days without the spinner playing a role, then picking one didn't hinder your team. And if you think it'll be a short match but it goes longer, then you have the resource that you need.
I'm told that the St George's Park band has been playing music for most of the morning, which is hilarious, but even they have stopped now. Tired out. The covers are coming off, though.
"Hello Geoff, thank you for your efforts in informing us about this almost game. I do hope they let you do your work from home!" In this case, yes, Mark Gretton, though more often I'm doing these updates from the ground.
"More pertinently, I was struck by the 'more in sorrow than in anger' tone of cricket SA after hardly anyone turned up to watch the first Test. I can save them money on their enquiry as to why that was: 1) finding the time of year when you can pretty much guarantee there won't be an uninterrupted day's play and, overwhelmingly 2) this serving to reinforce the point you've made repeatedly over the the past few years that Test cricket is no longer that important to you. I'm not unsympathetic to Cricket SA as to why they have elevated T20 as their cash cow of choice. But to then don sack cloth and ashes regarding Test attendance suggests foolishness, dishonesty, or both."
Well, quite, and there's also the fact that there has been no Test cricket in the country for close to a couple of years, and they didn't bother telling anyone that it was back. All reports from Durban were that promotion was non-existent. And yes, we know that CSA are very short on cash and probably don't have much marketing budget, but it also is hard to believe that it would be highly expensive in a South African context to engage local workers for some postering or flyering or targeted online ads.
There is a tendency, for those of us who are obsessed with cricket, to imagine that everyone else knows about it too. How could they not know about the Return from Sandpaper series, right? But, truth is they didn't.
That XKCD comic about "average familiarity" could apply to our field as well.
I've pondered this a bit, since Lyon's very public show of dismay after missing out in Brisbane last summer. In a way, I like that he's so fired up about missing a Test, and I like that he's candid about having feelings instead of brushing over them. And I don't like the increasing attitude that spin is not effective enough, but pace bowling magically is.
At the same time, I wonder how justifiable it is to be furious about missing a game when you've played 140 of them, more than almost anyone in the history of the sport. Does that then become a display of ego, thinking you're more important than the decisions the team is making about how best to win a game, or more important than other players, because literally everyone else on your team has had less opportunity to play for Australia than you?
John Dean - an OBO reader, not Nixon's lawyer, though I suppose one could be both - has written in regarding my questions about the state of mind of N. Lyon.
"Sadly there isn't a small door behind a filing cabinet on the 71⁄2thfloor of a Manhattan building I can crawl into to enter the mind of the GOAT. However, I'd imagine as hard done by as he'd feel, he recognises no one has been more hard done by on selection than ScoBo. He'd be filthy, but not at Bayside's favourite son."
The rain radar that I can find doesn't look promising either. Apart from depicting clouds as giant bilious green snot-chunks, which is highly unappealing, it has these chunks circling about and not moving anywhere. The main piece is off to the east of Gqeberha, but the smaller part over the town is largely static both in the prior tracking and the projection, just shifting in small circles.
A bit of a dance went on with the covers, where they came off, umpires talked about an inspection, then the covers went on again. A tale as old as time.
If there was a draw, it wouldn't cost Australia much in WTC terms: less than one percent on the ratio count, compared to an Australian win. But it could cost South Africa a lot, more like five percent versus a South African win. Not to mention that Australia won the last series between these sides, so if there's a washout here, South Africa can't win the series or take the trophy, such as it is. It still doesn't have much of an identity, although hopefully it doesn't end up being named after two randomly plucked players.
Later, once South Africa finally get to bowl, which may be Day 3 at this stage, we'll have the return of Rabada. He was the main character at this ground eight years ago.
All of this rain will give Nathan Lyon more time to think. The more time lost from the match, the more it suits the Australian approach of four fast bowlers, because the less they'll need a spinner to carry any slow periods of play. But I'm curious about what he makes of the situation. Is he as angry as he was when left out for four quicks in Jamaica and Brisbane recently? On the third time in the last eight Tests that he's been fit for, is there a level of acceptance? Does it cause despondency?
Interested in any reader thoughts about the role of spin in the modern game, given that England don't bother picking a proper spinner most of the time either.
My sources at the ground confirm what everyone else's sources at the ground say, which is that it is now absolutely pouring down. This is not what qualifies as breaking news.
This was the risk of Test cricket in October, we're told by South Africans. More likely to have bad weather. In 2018, of course, this tour was played in March and even strayed into the first days of April. Seven of the last eight Australian visits started in February or March. But that can't happen anymore, because that would displease the IPL, whose owners want Australian players, and would displease Australian players who want to earn the extra slice from the IPL.
Well, perhaps more importantly it would deny that same chance to South African players, who need that extra payday much more urgently given how little they comparatively earn from their home board, or more realistically it would see a Test series shorn of anyone who got picked up by the IPL.
Does the rain mean we're doomed to have a draw? Not necessarily, given the speed at which Test cricket moves in this era. Even in Durban, which was an uncharacteristic grind of a match relative to many recently, they only played about 360 of a possible 450 overs. All the time lost to bad light didn't matter, and it wasn't a close-run thing to finish the game on day five. If wickets keep falling when we get some play, the rain may not matter. But that's only if it clears up and stays away after this morning.
Hello all. Yes, we managed 12.2 overs yesteday, but somehow it was still quite an eventful 12.2 overs. Another chapter in the Scott Boland story, anyway. He's a quiet testament to humility. Very odd that CA didn't put him up to speak to media last night. They didn't put anyone up, which is highly unusual.
The bad news for those wanting the next chapter of this tale is that it's still raining in Gqeberha. So the planned early start won't happen, nor will the normal start on time, nor will anything probably for the first couple of hours. The forecast is better later, and even yesterday we were anticipating losing the morning.
new_text:
That's it from us today, very glad we got some action in the evening session. Australia are in command heading into day three with the weather set fair for the remainder of the match. Join us tomorrow for a full day's play, hopefully! Ta for your company, goodnight.
Phew. Mulder survives the final over from Starc and that's the end of the action on day two. It looked at one point that we wouldn't get any play at all but in the end it was a gripping thirty over session. Australia took three more wickets and South Africa still have their captain at the crease, Temba Bavuma battling through to the close unbeaten on 41.
43rd over: South Africa 97-5 (Bavuma 41, Mulder 2)
42nd over: South Africa 96-5 (Bavuma 40, Mulder 2) Scott Boland has to settle for his four-fer for now. Say that ten times fast. Just a single to Bavuma off his last one of the day, he'll be back tomorrow to wreak more havoc. Starc is going to bowl the final over of the day.
41st over: South Africa 95-5 (Bavuma 39, Mulder 2) Starc beats Mulder with a ball that seams in and decks away at pace, how did that not take the shoulder of the bat?! Boland will bowl his last over of the day next up with the scent of a Michelle in his nostrils.
40th over: South Africa 92-5 (Bavuma 38, Mulder 0) Rickelton couldn't believe the catch had been snaffled and stood rooted for a good few seconds. Mulder replaces him... and is nearly pinned LBW first ball! He got a scratch on it that saves him for a rapid departure. Wicket maiden for Boland - he has 4-30 from 15 overs with five maidens. Cripes.
WICKET! Ryan Rickelton c Renshaw b Boland 31 (South Africa 92-5)
Matt Renshaw pulls off a stunner at first slip! Rickelton edges that man Scott Boland and for a second it looks like the chance is going to fly between Carey and Renshaw. The keeper doesn't go for it so Renshaw sticks out a late velcro paw and grasps it milimetres off the turf! He can't quite believe it himself. Boland has four wickets and Australia get the late breakthrough they wanted. They might still get another this evening...
39th over: South Africa 92-4 (Bavuma 38, Rickelton 31) Starc replaces Boland for a final burst on day two, he spears down a maiden to Bavuma. Can this pair make it the close unscathed?
38th over: South Africa 92-4 (Bavuma 38, Rickelton 31) Drop! The plan was hatched and the leg side trap set, Rickleton obliged with a flick off his hip to Cummins that went straight to Marnus at leg slip... it was on him too quickly and smashes him in the solar plexus before falling to the floor. A big chance goes begging. Salt, meet Wound. Rickelton gets on his tippies and punches on the up for four to close out the over.
37th over: South Africa 86-4 (Bavuma 37, Rickelton 26) Boland draws Rickelton forward and takes the edge but it squirts downwards and away past the cordon for four. Lewk in the bewk. The home fans are at their loudest now, DJ Otzi is being parped and hollered...
36th over: South Africa 81-4 (Bavuma 37, Rickelton 21) Ooof Madon! Cummins goes short and Bavuma slams him for SIX out of nowhere! What a shot that is! No attempt whatsoever to keep it down, the Proteas captain swats it away in style. There's a bit of a delay as the ball is fetched from outside the stadium, Big Pat will not like that. He repsonds with two dots to finish the over, South Africa chalk another one off.
35th over: South Africa 73-4 (Bavuma 30, Rickelton 20) Scott Boland replaces Webster and is on the hunt for more notches in the wickets column. Bang! Rickelton greets Boland's out of character loosener with the full treatment, cutting for four past point. A streaky two follows with a slice through the off side. Tricky conditions for batting made worse by the sun dipping in and out over the pitch.
34th over: South Africa 67-4 (Bavuma 30, Rickelton 14) Cummins spears in a maiden with the whole ground now in shadow. We are due to get 45 mins or so more play but with the sun going down rapidly that could be unlikely. A few more overs for Bavuma and Rickelton to get their head down and they can look back on a decent fightback. Ouch! Rickelton wears a short one in the ribs, pass the arnica.
33rd over: South Africa 66-4 (Bavuma 30, Rickelton 14) Rickelton has shown decent judgement since he arrived in the middle. Webster nibbles it about on a length and Alex Carey is up to the stumps but Rickleton abjures anything he doesn't need to get his bat down on. Oh, just as I type that he takes a risky single that might have seen him back in the sheds had there been a direct hit! That was a classic case of take a run for the shot - it was straight to mid off! Lucky lad.
32nd over: South Africa 65-4 (Bavuma 30, Rickelton 13) Cummins is around the wicket but both Bavuma and Rickelton work the angle to collect singles into the leg side. This partnership is now the longest and most lucrative of the South African innings, the Proteas need them to survive to stumps and go again tomorrow when the going should be much more batter friendly.
31st over: South Africa 62-4 (Bavuma 29, Rickelton 11) Webster stitches together his third maiden on the bounce but Bavuma only had to play at a grand total of two deliveries in the over. Straighten it up Beau, old son.
30th over: South Africa 62-4 (Bavuma 29, Rickelton 11) That's more like it. Rickelton plays the shot of the day to Cummins's first ball, driving on the up back past the Aussie captain for four. Rinse and repeat! Cummins goes full again a couple of balls later and Rickelton pings him wide of mid off for another welcome boundary. A nosebleed inducing eight runs off the over.
29th over: South Africa 54-4 (Bavuma 29, Rickelton 3) Another maiden to Webster, he has a ring field and is bowling stump to stump, targeting the stumps and front pad. Bavuma plays a couple of handsome drives but can't break through the field. Starc is done this time, Cummins is coming on for a bowl with the shadows lengthening across the outfield now.
28th over: South Africa 54-4 (Bavuma 29, Rickelton 3) Starc wasn't hooked, it's a change of ends for him. Oooosht! He has Bavuma hopping around the crease with a delivery that spits off a length at 92mph and snorts passed the edge.
27th over: South Africa 52-4 (Bavuma 28, Rickelton 2) Webster has two slips and a gully. Hazlewood would be bowling these overs under normal circumstances but he's off the field with illness. Webster does his job though and keeps the pressure well and truly on with a maiden to start.
26th over: South Africa 52-4 (Bavuma 28, Rickelton 2) Bavuma playing a lone hand at the moment, he guides Starc away for four with aplomb and then takes a single with a clip through midwicket. Beau Webster is going to replace Starc for the next over.
24th over: South Africa 47-4 (Bavuma 23, Rickelton 2) Shot! Starc sends down a searing 92.5mph delivery but Bavuma plays it as if he is a medium paced dobber, stepping forward and lasering it through the covers.
23rd over: South Africa 43-4 (Bavuma 19, Rickelton 2) Bavuma is offering some solidity, if he goes then the you fear the whole batting card could collapse. He plays late and drops a single into the leg side.
22nd over: South Africa 42-4 (Bavuma 18, Rickelton 2) Rickelton arrives in the middle with a rescue job needed. He didn't get any as opener in the first game and is in at six for this one. he gets off the mark straightaway with a tuck to square leg. South Africa are in the mire though.
WICKET! Matthew Breetzke c Carey b Starc 4 (South Africa 40-4)
Starc strikes in his first over of the day! Breetzke plays too far away from his body and feathers an edge through to Carey. Problems for the home side.
21st over: South Africa 40-3 (Bavuma 18, Breetzke 4) The tv pictures cut out for a few minutes but there's two off Boland's over as Bavuma clips tidil off his pads. Mitch Starc is coming on to replace Captain Pat.
20th over: South Africa 38-3 (Bavuma 16, Breetzke 4) Cummins looks dangerous but after three dots Breetzke tucks off his hip to get down the other end .Bavuma negotiates a horrible ball in at the ribs.
19th over: South Africa 36-3 (Bavuma 15, Breetzke 3) Bavuma leans on a full ball from Boland and collects four with a compact drive down the ground. Two more singles, this pair doing well to keep the scoreboard moving despite the pressure cooker hissing.
18th over: South Africa 30-3 (Bavuma 10, Breetzke 1) Bavuma takes another nifty single off Cummins to bring Breetzke on strike, the latter gets off the mark with a guide down past gully for a couple.
17th over: South Africa 27-3 (Bavuma 9, Breetzke 0) Boland dots up Bavuma for five deliveries in a row but can't manage the sixth as the batter takes a single into the leg side to keep strike for the next. It's a gripping battle out there, another wicket in this passage of play and the Proteas are really in the mire.
16th over: South Africa 26-3 (Bavuma 8, Breetzke 0) A maiden from Cummins but there is a leg bye to the total courtesy of Bavuma's diddy pads. The bad parp away and the whole ground is bathed in glorious sunshine. Boland is coming back for another examination.
15th over: South Africa 25-3 (Bavuma 8, Breetzke 0) Matthew Breetzke is the new batter, this guy is a serious talent and his team need something from him here. He survives the rest of Boland's over but looks a smidge nervous out there, feet in concrete for the final ball and he does well to keep it at bay.
WICKET! Marques Ackerman c Carey b Boland 6 (South Africa 25-3)
It's a beautiful afternoon in Gqeberha now and apparently the weather is set fair for the rest of the match. Will we have enough time to see a result?
Err you wouldn't bet against it! Ackerman plays a loose waft outside off stump while on the walk to Boland and he pays the price! A thin edge through to Carey and he's on his way.
14th over: South Africa 25-2 (Bavuma 8, Ackerman 6) Cummins is pounding in, his very first ball takes a chunk of Ackerman's shoulder and is caught by Carey diving forward behind the sticks... Australia don't even send it upstairs, they know that the bat was nowhere near it. Ackerman drops and runs for a quick single and Bavuma does well to block out the rest of a typically probing Cummins over.
13th over: South Africa 24-2 (Bavuma 8, Ackerman 5) Boland beats Bavuma's defensive poke with a beauty that nips back late and almost tickles the off bail too! An absolute stunner to start proceedings from Scotty too Hotty. Shot! Bavuma then unfurls a peach of a cover drive to bisect the field. Honours even. Test cricket, you can't beat it.
Temba Bavuma is going to face up to four balls from Scott Boland to kick off day two. Thank all the higher powers that we have got here, finally. PLAY!
Right then, here we go. Well done to the groundstaff at St George's Park who have battled the wet stuff all day. The sun is shining brightly now and we've got a potential 30.4 overs of play to get through.
"Buckets and buckets of saw dust being applied to the outfield in front of the Castle Corner" writes James Walker. "Can't wait to see if the ball lands there and sticks like a 9 iron landed on a wet green."
Walker also has some goss:
"Was at the pub for lunch earlier and the owner asked us did we know what time the cricket was finished? The Australian team had a booking at her other venue and she'd been told they might arrive at 3pm or 6pm. Cue jokes about texting Cummo to confirm. Seems like the boys weren't expecting any cricket to be played today. Maybe they hadn't figured on all the saw dust."
Some more news - Josh Hazlewood is poorly and won't take the field today. So when they do get on Australia will be a bowler short. It shouldn't trouble them too much on a severely truncated day and the suggestion is he should be good to go tomorrow.
Here we go! The umpires have spoken - all being well we will have play at 3:45pm local time, just 25 minutes from now. There are 30.4 overs as a maximum and we'll be lucky to get all of them in with the light but heck, we'll take anything right about now.
More good news from Gqeberha! The players have arrived at the ground having been at the hotel all day. Buckle up folks, we could well have some Test cricket to watch in the not too distant.
I tell you what though, there are promising signs at the ground, the stumps are being readied and pitch lines painted! Hopefully we will see some action in a little over half an hour, wouldn't that be something!?
